newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB H1 profit seen up 4.5 pct amidst Bakun worries.
newsitem.headline: ABB H1 profit seen up 4.5 pct amidst Bakun worries.

text.p: Half-year results by ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG should confirm the trend toward improving profitability this year and next, but fresh doubt over Malaysia's Bakun project -- at $2.5 billion the largest order ever awarded to ABB -- threatens to steal the show.
Industry analysts are still uncertain about the fallout from Bakun but are looking to ABB to ease their worries and stem the flow of unsettling news from Malaysia and the Asian region.
"I am already assuming that Bakun won't be a best-case scenario for ABB," said Paola Orler of Zurich Kantonalbank.

ABB's six-month results on Thursday are unlikely to include any statement on the Bakun dispute, but at a briefing on Friday in London analysts are sure to press executives for clarity on the dispute over Bakun, details of which are unclear.
"There is a lot of interest in the Bakun project and its finance terms," said Russ Mould of SBC Warburg.

But ABB's first-half results, to be released around 1000 GMT, are expected to reflect the gradual improvement in its profits this year and reiterate its expectations of a recovery in earnings during the next two years.
On average 14 analysts in Stockholm, Zurich and London forecast a 4.5 percent growth in first-half group net profit to $581 million with a range from $511 million to $600 million.
"The results will neither be disastrous nor marvellous, but you never know," said Susan Anthony of Schroder Securities.
The higher dollar will tend to depress ABB's group results, which are reported in dollars, but inflate the earnings of its two, quoted parent companies, Swiss ABB AG and Sweden's ABB AB.
The rumble from Bakun comes on the heels of currency turbulence in many Asian countries, notably Thailand, and signs the region's rapid economic growth rate will ease.

Last week Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad said the government might intervene to resolve a dispute between ABB and the main developer of the $6.18 billion Bakun dam and there was a remote possibility the contract would be cancelled.

"The Bakun hydroelectric dam contract is the largest ever awarded to ABB with a value that exceeds $2.5 billion. ABB's portion of the work includes supplying hydro-generators, high voltage direct-current transmission systems and installing a submarine cable and other civil engineering works.

In the event of a cancellation, Francine Lenoir of Societe Generale said ABB would receive some indemnity and any impact on its share price would largely be psychological rather than from any sharp earning's downgrades.
"It would be a good opportunity to buy on disappointing news about Bakun," Lenoir said, adding that a cancellation would have a maximum five percent negative impact on earnings.
But analysts are anxious to hear ABB's views on Asian growth because it has a record of accurately reading and predicting economic changes, for example in Western Europe.
So far, however, analysts are not overly concerned.

Market expectations for ABB's half-year earnings are generally low-key, reflecting the company's own assessment of 1997 as a year of solid but unspectacular growth where net profit is only forecast to at least reach 1996's $1.233 billion.

Despite good growth in emerging markets, ABB is still suffering from the recent recession in Western Europe, still the mainstay of its business. Due to its late-cyclical nature, ABB's earnings will first start to reflect Europe's improving economy from 1998.
Analysts on average now look for a 5.0 percent increase in 1997 group net profit to $1.295 billion, slightly up from forecasts from April that called for $1.285 billion.
In 1998 ABB's profits are forecast to rise 21 percent on average to $1.572 billion as Europe's recovery takes hold. This forecast is unchanged from April.
Some 1997 earnings forecasts were tweaked upwards following ABB's first quarter results, which were better-than-expected and showed strong orders and an improving Power Generation segment.
These results comforted analysts, who had slashed earnings forecasts by 10 percent following disappointing 1996 earnings, including a 39 percent plunge in operating earnings at Power Generation.
